The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ is given above. Find ${f}^{′}(5).$

${f}^{′}(5)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To compute ${f}^{′}(5),$ we need to find the slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ at $x=5.$

Let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ for $x\in [4,6].$ Notice that $x=5$ lies in this interval.

![](images/42/42b4ddb29283047bd7ea8141ee14c793607b6b79a18f5d599a93839aec5a77b5.png)

The slope of $y=f(x)$ on $x\in (4,6)$ is constant and equals

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{5-(-1)}{6-4}=\frac{6}{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(5)=3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e6d75a63-b626-59fc-9980-1c756d4b224f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e6d75a63-b626-59fc-9980-1c756d4b224f" :answer-field/id #uuid "e6d75a63-b626-59fc-9980-1c756d4b224f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-75b7cdb7-77d7-57c2-97b3-ea13b000c118" :answer-field/choices ["answer-75b7cdb7-77d7-57c2-97b3-ea13b000c118"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-75b7cdb7-77d7-57c2-97b3-ea13b000c118" :answer/id #uuid "75b7cdb7-77d7-57c2-97b3-ea13b000c118" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096805 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7b5f58b1-1ad2-5dc4-9868-fc9b1d7a5b07" "question-2177aae9-0cdc-5d1b-af35-640b6cd8ac62" "question-c089daaf-37cc-52fb-a2a0-6074ff898dc3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-7b5f58b1-1ad2-5dc4-9868-fc9b1d7a5b07" :question/id #uuid "7b5f58b1-1ad2-5dc4-9868-fc9b1d7a5b07" :question/math-academy-id "q-344801" :question/problem "![](images/34/34d404457497fea78bd8b4e03d9ab9f4cc270487f1c478cb52780748e52163d5.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(1)$ where $h(x)=f(x)+g(x).$

${h}^{′}(1)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)+{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(1)={f}^{′}(1)+{g}^{′}(1).
$$

Also, notice that $x=1$ corresponds to

- the interval $x\in (-1,2)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (-1,2)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](images/62/62c27964999163f87224059d85e5e6fe07a2e8b343e9fef1c34723bf9fbaaec1.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-1,2)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{1-(-2)}{2-(-1)}=1.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(1)=1.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-1,2)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{-2-1}{2-(-1)}=-1.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(1)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(1) & ={f}^{′}(1)+{g}^{′}(1) \\  & =1+(-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-62da2b0e-6f79-559d-970c-50f59887f217"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-62da2b0e-6f79-559d-970c-50f59887f217" :answer-field/id #uuid "62da2b0e-6f79-559d-970c-50f59887f217" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d" :answer/id #uuid "bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2177aae9-0cdc-5d1b-af35-640b6cd8ac62" :question/id #uuid "2177aae9-0cdc-5d1b-af35-640b6cd8ac62" :question/math-academy-id "q-48950" :question/problem "![](images/39/39431059174ad545642732d57f40689e13af962ed2bc091b86eb0d4f41717299.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(2)$ where $h(x)=-2f(x)+3g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=-2{f}^{′}(x)+3{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(2)=-2{f}^{′}(2)+3{g}^{′}(2).
$$

Also, notice that $x=2$ corresponds to 

- the interval $x\in (1,3)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (1,3)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](images/33/33082034fa45d3228168431e8263c5a9f2c557ce26a8d637596a1e4e6d47d314.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (1,3)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{2-1}{3-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{2}.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (1,3)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{3-(-1)}{3-1}=2.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(2)=2.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & =-2{f}^{′}(2)+3{g}^{′}(2) \\  & =(-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}+3\cdot 2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-35c71da5-9853-5681-9c08-756d15831853"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-35c71da5-9853-5681-9c08-756d15831853" :answer-field/id #uuid "35c71da5-9853-5681-9c08-756d15831853" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5eca6fcd-90ba-5a2f-8d34-1b77aaafcabf" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bf15a1e8-e7a4-5205-ae23-b7f853d480f9" "answer-2a4551c2-b59b-5eca-8184-42852e416633" "answer-5eca6fcd-90ba-5a2f-8d34-1b77aaafcabf" "answer-cf5ccd17-d0df-51f1-89a9-b104c78567ad" "answer-777a7f91-b566-5e10-aaf6-e26f1de7019a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bf15a1e8-e7a4-5205-ae23-b7f853d480f9" :answer/id #uuid "bf15a1e8-e7a4-5205-ae23-b7f853d480f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2a4551c2-b59b-5eca-8184-42852e416633" :answer/id #uuid "2a4551c2-b59b-5eca-8184-42852e416633" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5eca6fcd-90ba-5a2f-8d34-1b77aaafcabf" :answer/id #uuid "5eca6fcd-90ba-5a2f-8d34-1b77aaafcabf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf5ccd17-d0df-51f1-89a9-b104c78567ad" :answer/id #uuid "cf5ccd17-d0df-51f1-89a9-b104c78567ad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-777a7f91-b566-5e10-aaf6-e26f1de7019a" :answer/id #uuid "777a7f91-b566-5e10-aaf6-e26f1de7019a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c089daaf-37cc-52fb-a2a0-6074ff898dc3" :question/id #uuid "c089daaf-37cc-52fb-a2a0-6074ff898dc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-105501" :question/problem "![](images/a8/a8345270e511644cfb019099b907ecadff056f7efbd396e84d4313f3c3ab5817.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(3)$ where $h(x)=f(x)-2g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)-2{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(3)={f}^{′}(3)-2{g}^{′}(3).
$$

Also, notice that $x=3$ corresponds to

- the interval $x\in (2,4)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (0,4)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](images/09/09e4836acd54b814c1691c60003614d206fc2eee5cda6d7ad8d6222dd72d2d4f.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (2,4)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{-2-2}{4-2}=-2.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(3)=-2.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (0,4)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{-2-0}{4-0}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(3)=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(3) & ={f}^{′}(3)-2{g}^{′}(3) \\  & =-2-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b308e7df-567f-5cd4-b865-053b904c951e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-c31fc413-2779-5fad-acf9-ef1563b305fb" :question/id #uuid "c31fc413-2779-5fad-acf9-ef1563b305fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-344908" :question/problem "![](images/c4/c4fd9b46fdb02c23e04c50e437076d7a74f4823546b6608dbe537defb8a439fc.png)

Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find ${h}^{′}(-2)$ where $h(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$

${h}^{′}(-2)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-2)=\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}}.
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2)=1$ and $g(-2)=2.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-3,-1)$ equals $0.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-2)=0.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-3,1)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-2)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-2) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1)}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-87e6f39a-f3fa-5af8-9dc4-36fec66a2e49"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-87e6f39a-f3fa-5af8-9dc4-36fec66a2e49" :answer-field/id #uuid "87e6f39a-f3fa-5af8-9dc4-36fec66a2e49" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa" :answer/id #uuid "c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-44024ffd-d823-5830-bedd-a0c95dfca83c" :question/id #uuid "44024ffd-d823-5830-bedd-a0c95dfca83c" :question/math-academy-id "q-344916" :question/problem "![](images/f5/f5f9c20bfeb54e816c98e75469f873d242b26143bdab65e56706861d8cbd7384.png)

Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find ${h}^{′}(-2)$ where $h(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$

${h}^{′}(-2)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-2)=\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}}.
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2)=3$ and $g(-2)=2.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-3,-1)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-2)=-1.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-3,-1)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-2)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-2) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 2-3\cdot (-1)}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-652c2813-5b15-52c4-be47-c3ffda7fdd27"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-652c2813-5b15-52c4-be47-c3ffda7fdd27" :answer-field/id #uuid "652c2813-5b15-52c4-be47-c3ffda7fdd27" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab" :answer/id #uuid "ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105854 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2e570ac4-c7f5-5887-a19e-4808c72f9d67"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2e570ac4-c7f5-5887-a19e-4808c72f9d67" :question/id #uuid "2e570ac4-c7f5-5887-a19e-4808c72f9d67" :question/math-academy-id "q-99288" :question/problem "Given that $p(x)=2x$ and $q(x)=7{x}^{4},$ what is ${lim}_{x\to \infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x))?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we multiply the two functions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x)) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(2x\cdot 7{x}^{4}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }((2\cdot 7){x}^{1+4}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(14\cdot {x}^{5}) \\  & =14\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{5}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5}=\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $14$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}14\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5} &={lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5}=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }(14{x}^{5})=\infty .
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-38288899-0ba2-57a8-830a-6a41d6af74e4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-d9945bb2-9891-5ac6-bca2-13e5bf3bd964" :question/id #uuid "d9945bb2-9891-5ac6-bca2-13e5bf3bd964" :question/math-academy-id "q-302063" :question/problem "If $p(x)=3{x}^{6}$ and $q(x)=4x,$ then

${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{p(x)}{{x}^{5}\cdot q(x)}=$
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, let's calculate ${x}^{5}\cdot q(x):$

$$
{x}^{5}\cdot q(x)={x}^{5}\cdot (4x)=4{x}^{6}.
$$

When we divide the two functions $p(x)$ and ${x}^{5}\cdot q(x),$ we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{p(x)}{{x}^{5}\cdot q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{3{x}^{6}}{4{x}^{6}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}

"What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the sequence

$$
f(n+1)=f(n)-\frac{3}{4},\,\,f(1)=-\frac{5}{4},\,\,n\ge 1?
$$" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

$$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is $f(1)=-\frac{5}{4},$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(1)-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =f(2)-f(1) \\  & =-2-(-\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $f(1)=-\frac{5}{4}$ and $d=-\frac{3}{4}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}+(n-1)(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}-\frac{3}{4}n+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}n-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=-\frac{3}{4}n-\frac{1}{2},\,n\ge 1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cdc27b07-45b8-5bb2-9278-1c5be0b7fdfb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199559 :tutorial/content "The **minimum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\min} \in S$ such that 

$$
x_{\min} \leq x
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the minimum is the element of $S$ that is *smaller than or equal to* any other element.

Similarly, the **maximum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\max} \in S$ such that 

$$
x \leq x_{\max}
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the maximum is the element of $S$ that is *larger than or equal to* any other element.

For example, what are the minimum and maximum of the following set? 

$$
A = \big\{ 2, \: -\sqrt{5}, \: 3, \: -1 \big\}
$$

Note that $-\sqrt{5} \approx -2.236.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}min(A) & =min\{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1\}=-\sqrt{5} \\ max(A) & =max\{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1\}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Some sets may not have a maximum or minimum. 

For example, consider the semi-open interval of real numbers $B=[1, 5).$ In this case, we have

$$
\min(B) = \min[1, 5) = 1.
$$

However, since $5 \notin B,$ the set has no maximum!

Finally, note the following:

- The maximum and minimum elements *must* belong to the underlying set.

- If the maximum or minimum elements exist, they are unique. In other words, there can be, at most, only one maximum and only one minimum.

- If the "less than or equal to" operation is not defined *for all* elements of a set $S,$ then the set has no maximum or minimum. For example, the following set has no minimum and maximum:

$$
S = \big\{\mathbb R, \clubsuit, 2, 3, \langle 1, 2, 3\rangle \big\}

$$
\sqrt[6]{x}\ge 0.
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. Hence,

$$
\sqrt[6]{4-3x}\ge 0.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-4$ and then adding $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[6]{4-3x} & \ge 0 \\ -4\sqrt[6]{4-3x} & \le 0 \\ -4\sqrt[6]{4-3x}+2 & \le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,2].$

{:db/id 17592186153395 :tutorial/content "**De Morgan's laws** for sets tell us alternative ways to represent the complement of a union or intersection.

- De Morgan's law for unions states that

$$
\overline{A \cup B} \equiv \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}.
$$

- De Morgan's law for intersections states that

$$
\overline{A \cap B} \equiv \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}.
$$

Intuitively, you can think that the complement "flips" the union into an intersection and vice versa.

To demonstrate De Morgan's laws, consider the sets $A = \{ 1,2,3 \}$ and $B = \{ 3,4 \}$ in the universe $U = \{ 1,2,3,4,5,6 \}.$

- Computing $\overline{A \cup B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A\cup B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}\cup \{3,4\}} \\  & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3,4\}} \\  & =\{5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\overline{A} \cap \overline{B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}}\cap \overset{―}{\{3,4\}} \\  & =\{4,5,6\}\cap \{1,2,5,6\} \\  & =\{5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $\overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- Computing $\overline{A \cap B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A\cap B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}\cap \{3,4\}} \\  & =\overset{―}{\{3\}} \\  & =\{1,2,4,5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\overline{A} \cup \overline{B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A}\cup \overset{―}{B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}}\cup \overset{―}{\{3,4\}} \\  & =\{4,5,6\}\cup \{1,2,5,6\} \\  & =\{1,2,4,5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $\overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152372 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105715 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-73a6be96-270e-560a-af2f-74b977e32a10"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-73a6be96-270e-560a-af2f-74b977e32a10" :question/id #uuid "73a6be96-270e-560a-af2f-74b977e32a10" :question/math-academy-id "q-49065" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{1}{3}$ out of the integral. $$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x})\text{d}x & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}+10\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =10(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}} \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}

"Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1-\frac{2}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1-\frac{4}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+4\cdot \frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{4}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-4\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1-\frac{2}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-4\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fc9d886d-2453-589c-b70a-85755f09affc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fc9d886d-2453-589c-b70a-85755f09affc" :answer-field/id #uuid "fc9d886d-2453-589c-b70a-85755f09affc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-41ec2527-87bc-5b8c-82c1-12de45de080a" "answer-33746465-e717-5154-b425-3b9867de6dcc" "answer-1c759ace-fa8b-5d0e-a8eb-8ecf03fcdc4a" "answer-0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" "answer-c6661073-9fee-582c-ad8c-e2b7b6a4e998"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-41ec2527-87bc-5b8c-82c1-12de45de080a" :answer/id #uuid "41ec2527-87bc-5b8c-82c1-12de45de080a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|1-\frac{2}{x}|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-33746465-e717-5154-b425-3b9867de6dcc" :answer/id #uuid "33746465-e717-5154-b425-3b9867de6dcc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1c759ace-fa8b-5d0e-a8eb-8ecf03fcdc4a" :answer/id #uuid "1c759ace-fa8b-5d0e-a8eb-8ecf03fcdc4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x-\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" :answer/id #uuid "0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6661073-9fee-582c-ad8c-e2b7b6a4e998" :answer/id #uuid "c6661073-9fee-582c-ad8c-e2b7b6a4e998" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107147 :tutorial/content "For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C = \ln K,$ where $K>0$ is some other constant. :question/problem "Given that $h(x,y)=({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇h(x,y)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =2x{e}^{x}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =-2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y)=({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇h(x,y)=0:$

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} &=0, \\ -2y{e}^{x} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{0}^{2}){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x(x+2){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0$ at two points: $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-73231a02-8c67-5ffc-9fab-d156f24315bc"] :db/ensure $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=f\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,f
$$

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\text{ }j=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =({e}^{x+y})(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})({e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =2x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a21aceed-9468-56fb-b467-8df32c0f6017"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2bb97214-9396-5a5e-8c44-9c78f53576a9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id is analogous to the derivative of a single-variable function.

For a function $f(x,y)$ whose partial derivatives exist at a point $(x,y),$ the **gradient vector** is denoted $\nabla f(x,y)$ and can be found by computing the vector of partial derivatives:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f (x,y) &=\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125727 :tutorial/content "For a function of three variables $f(x,y,z)$, the gradient of $f$ is given by the vector  

 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \! f (x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z (x,y,z)\ \mathbf k.
                             
\end{aligned}
$$

 

For a function $f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$ of $n$ variables, its gradient is usually given as a column vector:

![](images/21/21e05d85506da576e293bce86b1ca98f4f5b101c49b0591a49d80d2a4b8bfcc1.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115321 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e93fe40f-a4aa-5acf-8d5c-2ac8fa4691b8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e93fe40f-a4aa-5acf-8d5c-2ac8fa4691b8" :question/id #uuid "e93fe40f-a4aa-5acf-8d5c-2ac8fa4691b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-25487" :question/problem "Which of the following number lines represents the values of $w$ that satisfy $3w-7\le 5$ or $5w+7\ge -3$, or $2w<8?$" :question/worked-solution "We start by solving $3w-7\le 5:$

"d75d5c4d-ca96-55cd-81ad-3a4ef4cad6d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-95096" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$" :question/worked-solution "Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-805c950a-cc3b-53ae-82fe-bf9e8c3510ea"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/problem "$\int \frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Factoring out the constant $\frac{\pi }{2}$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get

is a positive real number, then the derivative of $a^x$ is given by

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm d x}\left( a^ x\right)	=	a^ x \ln a.
$$

So, by "reversing" this process, we obtain the following formula for the integral of a general exponential function:

$$
\displaystyle \int  a^x \, \textrm d x  = \dfrac{a^ x }{\ln a} +C.
$$

For instance, suppose that we wish to calculate the integral 

$$
\int 2^x  \, \textrm d x
$$

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int 2^x  \, \textrm d x   &= \dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2} + C
\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064408 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129163 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a616ae7d-06cd-5d59-abb1-f0bb3d95b238" "question-b089fead-c3aa-5630-9094-3b342b5bd931"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-a616ae7d-06cd-5d59-abb1-f0bb3d95b238" :question/id #uuid "a616ae7d-06cd-5d59-abb1-f0bb3d95b238" :question/math-academy-id "q-71569" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=9.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

:question/worked-solution "We can calculate the surface area of a sphere using the formula

$$
S=4\pi {r}^{2},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $S=144\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}$ into the above formula, we can solve for $r$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 144\pi  & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{144\pi }{4\pi } & ={r}^{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6\,\text{in}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we  can find the volume of the sphere as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi (6)^{3} \\  & =288\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}.\end{aligned}

![](images/bd/bd7da8538c268a1dd9e17dc8f4185ba3db5847dca21d1eb408d0af2683ba64d4.png)

We can calculate the surface area $S$ of a sphere using the formula

$$
S = 4\pi r^2,
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting $r=4\:\textrm{cm}$ into the formula, we obtain

$$
S = 4 \pi (4)^2
   = 64\pi \:\textrm{cm}^2.
$$

We often express the surface area of a sphere as a multiple of $\pi.$ We can also get a numerical approximation using a calculator. In this case, we have

$$
S \approx 201.06 \:\textrm{cm}^2
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119990 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119854 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cc7e6aad-0683-5027-b3d4-db532b43dae8" "question-d6a42f32-3ff1-5799-9155-413fd42c36ff"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-cc7e6aad-0683-5027-b3d4-db532b43dae8" :question/id #uuid "cc7e6aad-0683-5027-b3d4-db532b43dae8" :question/math-academy-id "q-74011" :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$

$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=2 \\ -5{x}_{2}+11{x}_{3} &=-4 \\ 4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -5 & 11 & -4 \\ 4 & -1 & -2 & 15\end{bmatrix}
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -5 & 11 & -4 \\ 4 & -1 & -2 & 15\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -5 & 11 & -4 \\ 0 & 7 & -14 & -7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -14 & -7 \\ 0 & -5 & 11 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & 11 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=2 \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=1.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}-2(1)=1\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=3.
$$

Finally, by substituting ${x}_{2}=3$ and ${x}_{3}=1$  into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-2(3)+3(1)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5.
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=5$, ${x}_{2}=3$, and ${x}_{3}=1,$ which means 

$$
5{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=5+3+1=9.

The first term that exceeds $2\,000\,000$ is the
{{field-1}}th term." :question/worked-solution "The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=2$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{2}=\sqrt{5}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\sqrt{5})}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {5}^{(n-1)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2\,000\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >2\,000\,000 \\ 2\cdot {5}^{(n-1)/2} & >2\,000\,000 \\ {5}^{(n-1)/2} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{(n-1)/2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ \frac{(n-1)}{2}\cdot \operatorname{log}⁡(5) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ \frac{(n-1)}{2} & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ n-1 & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ n & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}+1≈18.168.
$$

Therefore, the $19$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\,000\,000.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-82f102b3-cfde-50a7-befa-6d1aba4b3795"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-82f102b3-cfde-50a7-befa-6d1aba4b3795" :answer-field/id #uuid "82f102b3-cfde-50a7-befa-6d1aba4b3795" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-7f43b9ff-c57d-5176-8447-e1c240ac0c06" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7f43b9ff-c57d-5176-8447-e1c240ac0c06"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7f43b9ff-c57d-5176-8447-e1c240ac0c06" :answer/id #uuid "7f43b9ff-c57d-5176-8447-e1c240ac0c06" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "19" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ac65bd0d-2582-576c-9ae6-671d41f53032" :question/id #uuid "ac65bd0d-2582-576c-9ae6-671d41f53032" :question/math-academy-id "q-277938" :question/problem "What is the first term that exceeds  $1\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$" :question/worked-solution "The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=3$ and the common ratio is

term of this sequence to exceed $10\,000$ is the{{field-1}} th term." :question/worked-solution "Since we are given that ${a}_{3}=18$ and ${a}_{6}=486$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{6-3} & =\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{486}{18} \\ {r}^{3} & =27 \\ r & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{3}=18$ and  $r=3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{3-1} \\ 18 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{2} \\ 18 & =9{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $10\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {3}^{n-1} & >10\,000 \\ {3}^{n-1} & >5\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+1≈8.753.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{5}{4})}^{3-1} \\ 200 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\ 200 & =\frac{25}{16}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =128\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =128\cdot {(\frac{5}{4})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $8\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}128\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >8\,000 \\ {(\frac{5}{4})}^{n-1} & >62.5 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{5}{4})}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4})}+1≈19.531.
$$

Therefore, the $20$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $8\,000.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fa757127-e918-5b58-b712-d77618d9d911"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fa757127-e918-5b58-b712-d77618d9d911" :answer-field/id #uuid "fa757127-e918-5b58-b712-d77618d9d911" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-08c2b08f-4b86-5a28-b207-246ddaeede47" :answer-field/choices ["answer-08c2b08f-4b86-5a28-b207-246ddaeede47"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-08c2b08f-4b86-5a28-b207-246ddaeede47" :answer/id #uuid "08c2b08f-4b86-5a28-b207-246ddaeede47" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186093400 :tutorial/content "Consider the following geometric sequence: 

$$
3,\quad 6,\quad 12,\quad 24, \quad \ldots
$$

 

Suppose we want to find the first term that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$ We can do this by creating and solving an inequality.

First, let's construct a formula for the $n$th term of the sequence. The first term of the sequence is $a_1=3,$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac 6 3 = 2.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $3\,000\,000.$ So, we can set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >3\,000\,000 \\ 3\cdot {2}^{n-1} & >3\,000\,000 \\ {2}^{n-1} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({2}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (1\,000\,000)} {\log (2)} + 1 \approx 20.932.
$$

Therefore, the $21$st term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$

To check our answer, we can easily verify that $a_{20} < 3\, 000\, 000$ and $a_{21} > 3\, 000\, 000\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{20} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{20-1}=3\cdot {2}^{19}=1\,572\,864<3\,000\,000 \\ {a}_{21} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{21-1}=3\cdot {2}^{20}=3\,145\,728>3\,000\,000\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $a_{21}$ is indeed the first term that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092398 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083387 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b7cd0468-ad38-596e-ad84-07e63c57d66b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b7cd0468-ad38-596e-ad84-07e63c57d66b" :question/id #uuid "b7cd0468-ad38-596e-ad84-07e63c57d66b" :question/math-academy-id "q-288807" :question/problem "Consider the quadratic equation

**Without** solving the equation, determine the sum of its solutions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a=1,\,b=-83,\,c=1\,720.
$$

Therefore, the sum of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{b}{a} & =-\frac{(-83)}{1}=83.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e266ed12-ce03-5365-bb09-c240fd5249db"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Applying the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\cdot {3}^{x}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({3}^{x}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

                    

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{x}{|}_{x=1} \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{1} \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a8dd7b69-cfda-51dc-9216-0f0346dfcc24"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which of the following could be the equation of the polynomial curve shown above?" :question/worked-solution "First, we notice that the function has precisely three distinct roots, $x=-4$, $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots:

- Since the graph passes through $x=-4,$ this root has odd multiplicity, and since the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=-4,$ the multiplicity must be greater than one.

- Since the graph passes through $x=-1,$ this root has odd multiplicity, and since the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=-1,$ the multiplicity must be greater than one.

- Since the graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=1,$ this root is also a simple root (the multiplicity equals $1$).

From the given options, the only possible equation is $y=(x+4)^{3}(x+1)^{3}(x-1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields Which of the above could be the graph of $y=-x(x+1)(x+3)^{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "Based on the factored equation, we can make the following conclusions about the graph:

- Since the multiplicity of the roots $x=-1,0$ is $1,$ which is odd, the graph must cross the $x$-axis at these points. Moreover, because $x=-1,0$ are simple roots, the graph must *not* be tangent to the $x$-axis at these points.

- Since the multiplicity of the root $x=-3$ is $2,$ which is even, the graph just touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at this point.

Only the graphs $\text{I}$ and $\text{IV}$ satisfy these conditions.

To choose between these two graphs, we need to consider the end behavior. Since the leading coefficient is negative, as $x$ approaches $\infty ,$ $y$ approaches $-\infty .$

Only graph $\text{IV}$ displays this end behavior. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative using the product rule and sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(-4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+6) \\  & =\frac{d}{dx}(-4{e}^{x})\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x+(-4{e}^{x})\cdot \frac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\frac{d}{dx}(6) \\  & =-4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+(-4{e}^{x})(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)+0 \\  & =-4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\  & =-4{e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}⁡x(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and evaluate the slope $m:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={g}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-4{e}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-4{e}^{\pi /2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f569b9ca-3244-52df-8874-0fe9df4d2496"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f569b9ca-3244-52df-8874-0fe9df4d2496" :answer-field/id #uuid "f569b9ca-3244-52df-8874-0fe9df4d2496" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f17b38c0-319c-5a6b-a4a9-b68ba9b75662" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f17b38c0-319c-5a6b-a4a9-b68ba9b75662"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f17b38c0-319c-5a6b-a4a9-b68ba9b75662" :answer/id #uuid "f17b38c0-319c-5a6b-a4a9-b68ba9b75662" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4e^{\pi/2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116473 :tutorial/content "The derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions are shown in the table below:

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\sec x$ | $\sec x\tan x$ |
| $\csc x$ | $-\csc x\cot x$ |
| $\cot x$ | $-\csc^2 x$ |

As with the standard trigonometric functions, we can now differentiate any combination of the above functions using the rules of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of 

$$
y= \sec x + \csc x.
$$

We can take the derivative of each term and then add them, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csc}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We could have computed the derivative of the above function by rewriting it as

$$
y= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} + \dfrac{1}{\sin x}
$$

and applying the appropriate derivative rules. However, this would have taken significantly more work! You can save a lot of time by memorizing the derivatives of the reciprocal trigonometric functions." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116524 :tutorial/content "Trigonometric functions appear very frequently in calculus, so it's extremely important to commit their derivatives to memory.

Conveniently, there are some mnemonic tricks that we can use to more easily remember the derivatives of trigonometric functions.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x) & =-{csc}^{2}⁡x\, & \,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csc}⁡x) & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

It's helpful to notice that the "co"-functions (cosine, cosecant, and cotangent) all have negative signs in their derivatives, while the other trigonometric functions (sine, secant, and tangent) do not.

It's also helpful to realize that functions come in pairs.

- Sine and cosine are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

- Tangent and secant are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

- Cotangent and cosecant are a pair because each appears in the other's derivative.

Lastly, it's helpful to realize the following:

- Ignoring the positive or negative sign, tangent and cotangent have a similar format for their derivatives: the square of the function they're paired with.

- Ignoring the positive or negative sign, secant and cosecant have a similar format for their derivatives: the product of themself and the function they're paired with." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116474 :tutorial/content "To see why the derivative of $\sec x$ is $\sec x \tan x,$ we start by remembering that

$$
\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}.
$$

If we now differentiate the above relation using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x-1\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{{[\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(0)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x-1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={{\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}_{⏟}}_{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{{\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}_{⏟}}_{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the same method to find the derivative of the other two reciprocal trigonometric functions,

$$
\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115457 :activity/expected-seconds 1320.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060422 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059691 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ecab2b8f-98e3-5f6d-b4a6-b5491b118c68" "question-125cbfce-91f0-5374-bd89-78fd1d13de57"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ecab2b8f-98e3-5f6d-b4a6-b5491b118c68" :question/id #uuid "ecab2b8f-98e3-5f6d-b4a6-b5491b118c68" :question/math-academy-id "q-183294" :question/problem "Find the converse of the following statement:

:question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060985 :tutorial/content "A conditional statement $A \Rightarrow B$ has three related logical forms:

- the **converse:** $B \Rightarrow A$

- the **inverse:** $\lnot A \Rightarrow \lnot B$

- the **contrapositive:** $\lnot B \Rightarrow \lnot A$

For example, consider the following true statement:

$\qquad$ If I am George Washington, then I am an American.

Here, the antecedent is $A=$ "I am George Washington," and the consequent is $B=$ "I am an American."

- The *converse* is "If I am an American, then I am George Washington."

- The *inverse* is "If I am not George Washington, then I am not an American."

- The *contrapositive* is "If I am not an American, then I am not George Washington."

As we can see from the statements above, only the contrapositive is also true." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060986 :tutorial/content "In general, we have the following facts:

- The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original statement:

$$
\underbrace{A \Rightarrow B}_{\textrm{original}} \equiv \underbrace{\neg B \Rightarrow \neg A}_{\textrm{contrapositive}}
$$

- The inverse and the converse are logically equivalent to each other but not to the original statement:

$$
\underbrace{\neg A \Rightarrow \neg B}_{\textrm{inverse}} \equiv \underbrace{B \Rightarrow A}_{\textrm{converse}}
$$

The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find ${h}^{′}(1)$ where $h(x)=f(x)+g(x).$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)+{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(1)={f}^{′}(1)+{g}^{′}(1).
$$

Also, notice that $x=1$ corresponds to

- the interval $x\in (-1,2)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (-1,2)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](images/62/62c27964999163f87224059d85e5e6fe07a2e8b343e9fef1c34723bf9fbaaec1.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-1,2)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{1-(-2)}{2-(-1)}=1.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(1)=1.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-1,2)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{-2-1}{2-(-1)}=-1.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(1)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(1) & ={f}^{′}(1)+{g}^{′}(1) \\  & =1+(-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-62da2b0e-6f79-559d-970c-50f59887f217"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-62da2b0e-6f79-559d-970c-50f59887f217" :answer-field/id #uuid "62da2b0e-6f79-559d-970c-50f59887f217" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d" :answer/id #uuid "bc068b36-e83d-5fd2-9112-e63718de7e7d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2177aae9-0cdc-5d1b-af35-640b6cd8ac62" :question/id #uuid "2177aae9-0cdc-5d1b-af35-640b6cd8ac62" :question/math-academy-id "q-48950" :question/problem "![](images/39/39431059174ad545642732d57f40689e13af962ed2bc091b86eb0d4f41717299.png)

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-2)=\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}}.
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2)=1$ and $g(-2)=2.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-3,-1)$ equals $0.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-2)=0.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-3,1)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-2)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-2) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1)}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-87e6f39a-f3fa-5af8-9dc4-36fec66a2e49"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-87e6f39a-f3fa-5af8-9dc4-36fec66a2e49" :answer-field/id #uuid "87e6f39a-f3fa-5af8-9dc4-36fec66a2e49" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa" :answer/id #uuid "c875190b-c18b-5e5f-88f4-f546edcab3aa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-44024ffd-d823-5830-bedd-a0c95dfca83c" :question/id #uuid "44024ffd-d823-5830-bedd-a0c95dfca83c" :question/math-academy-id "q-344916" :question/problem "![](images/f5/f5f9c20bfeb54e816c98e75469f873d242b26143bdab65e56706861d8cbd7384.png)

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-2)=\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}}.
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2)=3$ and $g(-2)=2.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-3,-1)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-2)=-1.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-3,-1)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-2)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-2) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(-2)\cdot g(-2)-f(-2)\cdot {g}^{′}(-2)}{(g(-2))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 2-3\cdot (-1)}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-652c2813-5b15-52c4-be47-c3ffda7fdd27"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-652c2813-5b15-52c4-be47-c3ffda7fdd27" :answer-field/id #uuid "652c2813-5b15-52c4-be47-c3ffda7fdd27" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab" :answer/id #uuid "ffa62cc5-94c6-551b-96c6-16b6cd1270ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105854 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2e570ac4-c7f5-5887-a19e-4808c72f9d67"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2e570ac4-c7f5-5887-a19e-4808c72f9d67" :question/id #uuid "2e570ac4-c7f5-5887-a19e-4808c72f9d67" :question/math-academy-id "q-99288" :question/problem "Given that $p(x)=2x$ and $q(x)=7{x}^{4},$ what is ${lim}_{x\to \infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x))?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we multiply the two functions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x)) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(2x\cdot 7{x}^{4}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }((2\cdot 7){x}^{1+4}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(14\cdot {x}^{5}) \\  & =14\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{5}$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5}=\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $14$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}14\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5} &={lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{5}=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }(14{x}^{5})=\infty .
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-38288899-0ba2-57a8-830a-6a41d6af74e4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the sequence

$$
f(n+1)=f(n)-\frac{3}{4},\,\,f(1)=-\frac{5}{4},\,\,n\ge 1?
$$" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

$$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d,\,n\ge 1,
$$

so we need to determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is $f(1)=-\frac{5}{4},$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(1)-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =f(2)-f(1) \\  & =-2-(-\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $f(1)=-\frac{5}{4}$ and $d=-\frac{3}{4}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}+(n-1)(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}-\frac{3}{4}n+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}n-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=-\frac{3}{4}n-\frac{1}{2},\,n\ge 1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cdc27b07-45b8-5bb2-9278-1c5be0b7fdfb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

To complete the formula, we need to work out the first term and common difference. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =2(1)-1=1 \\ f(2) & =2(2)-1=3\end{aligned}
$$

and the common difference is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =f(2)-f(1) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(n+1)=f(n)+2,\,f(1)=1,\,n\ge 1

17592186199559 :tutorial/content "The **minimum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\min} \in S$ such that 

$$
x_{\min} \leq x
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the minimum is the element of $S$ that is *smaller than or equal to* any other element.

Similarly, the **maximum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\max} \in S$ such that 

$$
x \leq x_{\max}
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the maximum is the element of $S$ that is *larger than or equal to* any other element.

For example, what are the minimum and maximum of the following set? 

$$
A = \big\{ 2, \: -\sqrt{5}, \: 3, \: -1 \big\}
$$

Note that $-\sqrt{5} \approx -2.236.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}min(A) & =min\{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1\}=-\sqrt{5} \\ max(A) & =max\{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1\}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Some sets may not have a maximum or minimum. 

For example, consider the semi-open interval of real numbers $B=[1, 5).$ In this case, we have

$$
\min(B) = \min[1, 5) = 1.
$$

However, since $5 \notin B,$ the set has no maximum!

Finally, note the following:

- The maximum and minimum elements *must* belong to the underlying set.

- If the maximum or minimum elements exist, they are unique. In other words, there can be, at most, only one maximum and only one minimum.

- If the "less than or equal to" operation is not defined *for all* elements of a set $S,$ then the set has no maximum or minimum. For example, the following set has no minimum and maximum:

$$
S = \big\{\mathbb R, \clubsuit, 2, 3, \langle 1, 2, 3\rangle \big\}

$$
\sqrt[6]{x}\ge 0.
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. Hence,

$$
\sqrt[6]{4-3x}\ge 0.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-4$ and then adding $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[6]{4-3x} & \ge 0 \\ -4\sqrt[6]{4-3x} & \le 0 \\ -4\sqrt[6]{4-3x}+2 & \le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,2].$

{:db/id 17592186153395 :tutorial/content "**De Morgan's laws** for sets tell us alternative ways to represent the complement of a union or intersection.

- De Morgan's law for unions states that

$$
\overline{A \cup B} \equiv \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}.
$$

- De Morgan's law for intersections states that

$$
\overline{A \cap B} \equiv \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}.
$$

Intuitively, you can think that the complement "flips" the union into an intersection and vice versa.

To demonstrate De Morgan's laws, consider the sets $A = \{ 1,2,3 \}$ and $B = \{ 3,4 \}$ in the universe $U = \{ 1,2,3,4,5,6 \}.$

- Computing $\overline{A \cup B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A\cup B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}\cup \{3,4\}} \\  & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3,4\}} \\  & =\{5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\overline{A} \cap \overline{B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}}\cap \overset{―}{\{3,4\}} \\  & =\{4,5,6\}\cap \{1,2,5,6\} \\  & =\{5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $\overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- Computing $\overline{A \cap B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A\cap B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}\cap \{3,4\}} \\  & =\overset{―}{\{3\}} \\  & =\{1,2,4,5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\overline{A} \cup \overline{B},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A}\cup \overset{―}{B} & =\overset{―}{\{1,2,3\}}\cup \overset{―}{\{3,4\}} \\  & =\{4,5,6\}\cup \{1,2,5,6\} \\  & =\{1,2,4,5,6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $\overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152372 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105715 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-73a6be96-270e-560a-af2f-74b977e32a10"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-73a6be96-270e-560a-af2f-74b977e32a10" :question/id #uuid "73a6be96-270e-560a-af2f-74b977e32a10" :question/math-academy-id "q-49065" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{1}{3}$ out of the integral. $$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x})\text{d}x & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}+10\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =10(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}} \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}

"Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1-\frac{2}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1-\frac{4}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+4\cdot \frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{4}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-4\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1-\frac{2}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-4\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fc9d886d-2453-589c-b70a-85755f09affc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fc9d886d-2453-589c-b70a-85755f09affc" :answer-field/id #uuid "fc9d886d-2453-589c-b70a-85755f09affc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-41ec2527-87bc-5b8c-82c1-12de45de080a" "answer-33746465-e717-5154-b425-3b9867de6dcc" "answer-1c759ace-fa8b-5d0e-a8eb-8ecf03fcdc4a" "answer-0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" "answer-c6661073-9fee-582c-ad8c-e2b7b6a4e998"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-41ec2527-87bc-5b8c-82c1-12de45de080a" :answer/id #uuid "41ec2527-87bc-5b8c-82c1-12de45de080a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|1-\frac{2}{x}|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-33746465-e717-5154-b425-3b9867de6dcc" :answer/id #uuid "33746465-e717-5154-b425-3b9867de6dcc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1c759ace-fa8b-5d0e-a8eb-8ecf03fcdc4a" :answer/id #uuid "1c759ace-fa8b-5d0e-a8eb-8ecf03fcdc4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x-\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" :answer/id #uuid "0a9e1968-ebda-5b8a-87f8-c6f794e88a9a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6661073-9fee-582c-ad8c-e2b7b6a4e998" :answer/id #uuid "c6661073-9fee-582c-ad8c-e2b7b6a4e998" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107147 :tutorial/content "For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C = \ln K,$ where $K>0$ is some other constant. :question/problem "Given that $h(x,y)=({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇h(x,y)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =2x{e}^{x}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =-2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y)=({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇h(x,y)=0:$

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} &=0, \\ -2y{e}^{x} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{0}^{2}){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x(x+2){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0$ at two points: $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-73231a02-8c67-5ffc-9fab-d156f24315bc"] :db/ensure $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=f\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,f
$$

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\text{ }j=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =({e}^{x+y})(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})({e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =2x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a21aceed-9468-56fb-b467-8df32c0f6017"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2bb97214-9396-5a5e-8c44-9c78f53576a9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id is analogous to the derivative of a single-variable function.

For a function $f(x,y)$ whose partial derivatives exist at a point $(x,y),$ the **gradient vector** is denoted $\nabla f(x,y)$ and can be found by computing the vector of partial derivatives:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f (x,y) &=\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125727 :tutorial/content "For a function of three variables $f(x,y,z)$, the gradient of $f$ is given by the vector  

 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \! f (x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z (x,y,z)\ \mathbf k.
                             
\end{aligned}
$$

 

For a function $f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$ of $n$ variables, its gradient is usually given as a column vector:

![](images/21/21e05d85506da576e293bce86b1ca98f4f5b101c49b0591a49d80d2a4b8bfcc1.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115321 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e93fe40f-a4aa-5acf-8d5c-2ac8fa4691b8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e93fe40f-a4aa-5acf-8d5c-2ac8fa4691b8" :question/id #uuid "e93fe40f-a4aa-5acf-8d5c-2ac8fa4691b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-25487" :question/problem "Which of the following number lines represents the values of $w$ that satisfy $3w-7\le 5$ or $5w+7\ge -3$, or $2w<8?$" :question/worked-solution "We start by solving $3w-7\le 5:$

"d75d5c4d-ca96-55cd-81ad-3a4ef4cad6d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-95096" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$" :question/worked-solution "Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-805c950a-cc3b-53ae-82fe-bf9e8c3510ea"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/problem "$\int \frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Factoring out the constant $\frac{\pi }{2}$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get
