$$
\lim_{x \to \infty} x^3=\infty \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} x^3=-\infty.
$$

These limits are valid for any power function of the form $x^n,$ where $n$ is an *odd natural number*.

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^n=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^n=-\infty, \qquad n=1,3,5,\ldots.
$$

Again, multiplication of $x^n$ by a positive constant does not affect the limit at infinity. However, multiplication by a negative constant changes the sign of the limit." :tutorial/id #uuid "d9d4d60e-df4b-5dbb-85e6-e53ab24b16f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 192 :tutorial/title "Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power"} :step/id #uuid "c2cbae50-d421-561d-b4fe-f6dcc8a8591d" :step/math-academy-id 357 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106820}} {:db/id 17592186106820 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105854 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105565 :question/id #uuid "551f2aa0-8589-5725-abe6-de1b7eca0327" :question/math-academy-id "e-37"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a5bea806-2913-57f5-ba32-be7aeda5bd15" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106285} {:db/id 17592186106288} {:db/id 17592186233761} {:db/id 17592186233868} {:db/id 17592186233997} {:db/id 17592186297260} {:db/id 17592186311764} {:db/id 17592186311765} {:db/id 17592186320929} {:db/id 17592186562466} {:db/id 17592186562505}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power"} :step/id #uuid "800c9745-b1c3-57bb-8946-69f8df02ae03" :step/math-academy-id 358 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106560}} {:db/id 17592186106827 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107040 :tutorial/content "To compute the limit at infinity of a general polynomial, we *only* need to consider the term with the largest exponent, called the **leading term**. All of the other terms can be disregarded!

For example, to compute 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \infty} \left( 6x + 2x^3-7x^2+12\right) \, ,
$$

 we identify the leading term and compute its limit. Here, the leading term is ${\color{blue}{2x^3}},$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(6x+2{x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+12) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(2{x}^{3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{3}) \\  & =\infty \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The reason this works is that when $x$ becomes very large, the behavior of the polynomial is dominated by the term with the largest exponent.

**Watch out!** The leading term is *not* always the first term that appears in the expression. Rather, it is the term *with the largest exponent*. This term may appear anywhere in the expression.

The reason why we call the term with the largest exponent the "leading" term is that when the polynomial is arranged in standard form (with exponents ordered from greatest to least), the term with the largest exponent appears first:

$$
6x+ {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+12 \quad \to \quad {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+6x+12
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "549fd7b8-2367-5c38-b26e-475d7c827a1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 196 :tutorial/title "Limits at Infinity of General Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "5e48e500-3385-5631-9674-a6c6b177bfcd" :step/math-academy-id 363 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106828}} {:db/id 17592186106828 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105857 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105576 :question/id #uuid "969d5f07-c5ce-5601-b2de-0d23eb15809b" :question/math-academy-id "e-39"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fc04f720-28f3-55ab-8e89-582db57672a4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106303} {:db/id 17592186106452} {:db/id 17592186233545} {:db/id 17592186233759} {:db/id 17592186234000} {:db/id 17592186235412} {:db/id 17592186311782} {:db/id 17592186311783} {:db/id 17592186311784} {:db/id 17592186311785} {:db/id 17592186311786} {:db/id 17592186320803} {:db/id 17592186362357} {:db/id 17592186402402} {:db/id 17592186402675} {:db/id 17592186522796}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "923659ef-18ec-5fc8-8fb8-ff70ca00d5c0" :step/math-academy-id 364}] :activity/title "Limits at Infinity of Polynomials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105950} {:db/id 17592186106812 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107038 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to calculate $\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^2$ and $\lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^2.$ To do this, we can use the graph of $y=x^2,$ which takes the familiar shape of a parabola.

$$

![](images/5e/5e7386db15731b3486fd64484db69e7919c8e79821d916974f689d737cf23f8a.png)

In general, whenever $n$ is an *even natural number*, we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^n=\infty\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} x^n=\infty, \qquad \textrm{for}\qquad n=2,4,6,\ldots.

Likewise,

In general, for any constant $C,$ we have

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(6x+2{x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+12) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(2{x}^{3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{3}) \\  & =\infty \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The reason this works is that when $x$ becomes very large, the behavior of the polynomial is dominated by the term with the largest exponent.

**Watch out!** The leading term is *not* always the first term that appears in the expression. Rather, it is the term *with the largest exponent*. This term may appear anywhere in the expression.

The reason why we call the term with the largest exponent the "leading" term is that when the polynomial is arranged in standard form (with exponents ordered from greatest to least), the term with the largest exponent appears first:

$$
6x+ {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+12 \quad \to \quad {\color{blue}{2x^3}}-7x^2+6x+12
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "549fd7b8-2367-5c38-b26e-475d7c827a1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 196 :tutorial/title "Limits at Infinity of General Polynomials"} {:db/id 17592186106828 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134608 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135191 :tutorial/content "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

Every arithmetic sequence can also be written using the following recursive formula:

![](images/a2/a2d28772cb4cb6078d2fccdca054ec1c2dccf27a5ea0b5972b9ac174eaad671f.svg)

For example, suppose that we're given the following explicit formula for an arithmetic sequence:

$$
a_n =2n+6, \quad n\geq 1
$$

To convert to a recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common difference. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2(1)+6=8 \\ {a}_{2} & =2(2)+6=10,\end{aligned}
$$

and the common difference is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =10-8 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}8}$ and the common difference is $d={\color{red}2}.$ Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}2}, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}8}, \quad n \geq 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b6cd14c7-922b-5e05-9c8e-b842717155ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8910 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "02ae2395-79da-5dc3-9f17-a75936abdc07" :step/math-academy-id 191930 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134609}} {:db/id 17592186134609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133746 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133531 :question/id #uuid "00113d76-b950-513e-a3ea-29eef91c9cec" :question/math-academy-id "e-14383"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9b8b10a8-f81a-5dae-b54e-b10959e3ad14" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050157} {:db/id 17592186050380}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134163} {:db/id 17592186134446} {:db/id 17592186560987} {:db/id 17592186561011}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting an Explicit Formula to a Recursive Formula"} :step/id #uuid "ed82570d-8cc5-564d-8da6-d86c3395fced" :step/math-academy-id 191931 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134610}} {:db/id 17592186134610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133747 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133532 :question/id #uuid "e04ad3e0-888e-51c0-b60c-e816b7df514b" :question/math-academy-id "e-14386"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d36a3a61-e23b-5ce3-ac65-f7ac1691ec4e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134177} {:db/id 17592186134447} {:db/id 17592186560975} {:db/id 17592186561005}] :knowledge-point/title "Converting an Explicit Formula to a Recursive Formula Using Function Notation"} :step/id #uuid "340d50dc-babe-5074-be5e-52e39f437e88" :step/math-academy-id 191934 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134611}} {:db/id 17592186134611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135192 :tutorial/content "It's often more useful to translate from the recursive formula to an explicit one. So how do we find the explicit formula for the arithmetic sequence defined recursively as

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}1},\, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}6},\, \quad n\geq 1?
$$

The explicit formula is

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1,
$$

so we just need to determine the first term $a_1$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}6},$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+1 \\  & =6+1 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =7-6 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $a_1 = {\color{blue}6}$ and $d={\color{red}1}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\eqalign{
a_n&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
&= {\color{blue}6} + (n - 1)({\color{red}1}) \[3pt]
& =6 + n-1\[3pt]
&=n+5
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=n+5, \quad n \geq 1.

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

Every arithmetic sequence can also be written using the following recursive formula:

![](images/a2/a2d28772cb4cb6078d2fccdca054ec1c2dccf27a5ea0b5972b9ac174eaad671f.svg)

For example, suppose that we're given the following explicit formula for an arithmetic sequence:

$$
a_n =2n+6, \quad n\geq 1
$$

To convert to a recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common difference. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2(1)+6=8 \\ {a}_{2} & =2(2)+6=10,\end{aligned}
$$

and the common difference is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =10-8 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}8}$ and the common difference is $d={\color{red}2}.$ Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}2}, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}8}, \quad n \geq 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b6cd14c7-922b-5e05-9c8e-b842717155ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8910 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "02ae2395-79da-5dc3-9f17-a75936abdc07" :step/math-academy-id 191930 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134609}} {:db/id 17592186135191 :tutorial/content "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

So how do we find the explicit formula for the arithmetic sequence defined recursively as

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}1},\, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}6},\, \quad n\geq 1?
$$

The explicit formula is

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1,
$$

so we just need to determine the first term $a_1$ and the common difference $d.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}6},$ and we can use the recursive rule to compute the second term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}+1 \\  & =6+1 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Using the first and second terms, we can compute the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =7-6 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $a_1 = {\color{blue}6}$ and $d={\color{red}1}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\eqalign{
a_n&= a_{1}+(n-1)d \[3pt]
&= {\color{blue}6} + (n - 1)({\color{red}1}) \[3pt]
& =6 + n-1\[3pt]
&=n+5
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=n+5, \quad n \geq 1.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c5b9f8-4c71-5c1f-8841-3f22646e5074" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8914 :tutorial/title "Translating From the Recursive to the Explicit Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7cd53e1d-4c0c-570b-bef4-68f8081c2fef" :step/math-academy-id 191938 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134612}} {:db/id 17592186135192 :tutorial/content "It's often more useful to translate from the recursive formula to an explicit one. - $x_{\max}$ is the maximum of a set $S$ if $x_{\max} \in S$ and $x \leq x_{\max}$ for all $x \in S,$ and

- $x_{\min}$ is the minimum of a set $S$ if $x_{\min} \in S$ and $x_{\min} \leq x$ for all $x \in S.$

Notice that the elements of the set can be listed as 

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 4396} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199149 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199559 :tutorial/content "The **minimum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\min} \in S$ such that 

$$
x_{\min} \leq x
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the minimum is the element of $S$ that is *smaller than or equal to* any other element.

Similarly, the **maximum** of a set $S$ is the element $x_{\max} \in S$ such that 

$$
x \leq x_{\max}
$$

for all $x \in S.$ In other words, the maximum is the element of $S$ that is *larger than or equal to* any other element.

For example, what are the minimum and maximum of the following set? 

$$
A = \big\{ 2, \: -\sqrt{5}, \: 3, \: -1 \big\}
$$

Note that $-\sqrt{5} \approx -2.236.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}min(A) & =min{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1}=-\sqrt{5} \\ max(A) & =max{2,\,-\sqrt{5},\,3,\,-1}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Some sets may not have a maximum or minimum. 

For example, consider the semi-open interval of real numbers $B=[1, 5).$ In this case, we have

$$
\min(B) = \min[1, 5) = 1.
$$

However, since $5 \notin B,$ the set has no maximum!

Finally, note the following:

- The maximum and minimum elements *must* belong to the underlying set.

- If the maximum or minimum elements exist, they are unique. In other words, there can be, at most, only one maximum and only one minimum.

- If the "less than or equal to" operation is not defined *for all* elements of a set $S,$ then the set has no maximum or minimum. For example, the following set has no minimum and maximum:

$$
S = \big\{\mathbb R, \clubsuit, 2, 3, \langle 1, 2, 3\rangle \big\}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9377b093-e187-5c5e-9f3d-768297aaf57e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8236 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "dc18f60a-72ad-5caa-8d0b-2f93237f062b" :step/math-academy-id $$
f(x) = -2\sqrt[3]{3x-2}+2?
$$

What is the range of 

$$
g(x) = -3\sqrt[4]{2x-1}-2?
$$

The range of $\sqrt[4] x$ is

$$
\sqrt[4] x \ge 0.
$$

Now, let's apply transformations to the inequality above to turn the left-hand side into $g(x).$

First, remember that horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[4]{2x-1} \ge 0.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-3$ and then subtracting $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[4]{2x-1} & \ge 0 \\ -3\sqrt[4]{2x-1} & \le 0 \\ -3\sqrt[4]{2x-1}-2 & \le -2 \\ g(x) & \le -2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $g(x) \in (-\infty,-2].$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=g(x)$ is shown below.

:step/content {:db/id 17592186153395 :tutorial/content "**De Morgan's laws** for sets tell us alternative ways to represent the complement of a union or intersection.

- De Morgan's law for unions states that $$\overline{A \cup B} \equiv \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}.$$
- De Morgan's law for intersections states that $$\overline{A \cap B} \equiv \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}.$$

Intuitively, you can think that the complement "flips" the union into an intersection and vice versa.

To demonstrate De Morgan's laws, consider the sets $A = \{ 1,2,3 \}$ and $B = \{ 3,4 \}$ in the universe $U = \{ 1,2,3,4,5,6 \}.$

- Computing $\overline{A \cup B},$ we have $$\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A\cup B} & =\overset{―}{{1,2,3}\cup {3,4}} \\ & =\overset{―}{{1,2,3,4}} \\ & ={5,6}.\end{aligned}$$ Computing $\overline{A} \cap \overline{B},$ we have $$\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A}\cap \overset{―}{B} & =\overset{―}{{1,2,3}}\cap \overset{―}{{3,4}} \\ & ={4,5,6}\cap {1,2,5,6} \\ & ={5,6}.\end{aligned}$$ So, we have that $\overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$
- Computing $\overline{A \cap B},$ we have $$\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A\cap B} & =\overset{―}{{1,2,3}\cap {3,4}} \\ & =\overset{―}{{3}} \\ & ={1,2,4,5,6}.\end{aligned}$$ Computing $\overline{A} \cup \overline{B},$ we have $$\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A}\cup \overset{―}{B} & =\overset{―}{{1,2,3}}\cup \overset{―}{{3,4}} \\ & ={4,5,6}\cup {1,2,5,6} \\ & ={1,2,4,5,6}.\end{aligned}$$ So, we have that $\overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$" :tutorial/id #uuid "df8a49e7-15bf-53b1-9af3-754dbf9fc0e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4366 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1f2c991b-1f17-5ca9-b2bb-adab88ae5d59" :step/math-academy-id 26659 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153133}} {:db/id 17592186153133 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153396 :tutorial/content "For the sets $A = \{ 1,2,3 \}$ and $B = \{ 3,4 \}$ in the universe $U = \{ 1,2,3,4,5,6 \},$ the region $\overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cap \overline{B}$ is shown below:

$$
\int ({x}^{3/2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1})\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{\frac{3}{2}+1}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5/2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186297251 :question/id #uuid "a9a35970-b3a0-5bae-b863-30b3731d8d68" :question/math-academy-id "q-29885"} {:db/id 17592186297252 :question/id #uuid antiderivative of $\dfrac {3+2x} {x} ?$" :question/worked-solution "We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =3 \ln K$ where $K$ is some other constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+3ln⁡K \\  & =3ln⁡(K|x|)+2x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186485703} {:db/id 17592186106053 :question/id #uuid "4863b144-6916-5476-8b2b-08b73058b19d" :question/math-academy-id "q-15717"} {:db/id 17592186106365 :question/id #uuid $$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\ln{|x|}) = \dfrac 1 x.
$$

$$
\int \dfrac 1 x \,\textrm{d}x = \ln |x| + C.

:knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables"}] :question/problem "Find $\nabla f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,\pi)$ given that $f(x,y) = (x - y)\cos y.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y-(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the gradient at the specified point, we substitute $(x,y)= (1,\pi)$ into the above, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(1,\pi ) & ={f}_{x}(1,\pi )\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(1,\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +(1-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124940 :question/id #uuid "c9824799-8fb2-5e3e-9b52-a3b623c77e1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-35988" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124443 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =⟨{h}_{x}(x,y),\,{h}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y,\,\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ ∇h(1,1) & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡1,\,\frac{4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{4}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186323740 :question/id #uuid "4dc17c5e-dc05-517c-b33a-803dd069587a" :question/math-academy-id "q-36009"} {:db/id 17592186323860 :question/id #uuid "4b4ba176-5939-5525-9fa4-02ef800efbcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-36909" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124443 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e3991a54-342b-5cd0-87e2-606146240555" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25a66e67-c420-5bae-9224-c8f5d4fde075" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨4,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186321440} {:answer/id #uuid "47baee24-d042-549a-8151-b2da72dc39a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨2,\,0⟩" :db/id 17592186321711} {:answer/id #uuid "9abaf78d-69a4-535f-a08b-0a3417313ea2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨1,\,8⟩" :db/id 17592186322375} {:answer/id #uuid "c8af8076-8ba0-5745-9225-6f71fe87a617" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨16,\,1⟩" :db/id 17592186322707} {:answer/id #uuid "cc23bd77-b2ea-5ecd-832e-27ef06e5c5fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨8,\,1⟩" :db/id 17592186322734}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "cc23bd77-b2ea-5ecd-832e-27ef06e5c5fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨8,\,1⟩" :db/id 17592186322734} :answer-field/id #uuid "561a4834-955d-5829-ab93-034d86fd0c74" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186323334}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Evaluate $∇f(x,y)$ at $(2,1)$ if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =2x\sqrt{y+3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+(xz)\text{ }j+(xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇g(2,-1,3) & =(2(2)+(-1)(3))\text{ }i+2(3)\text{ }j+2(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =1\text{ }i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186551602} {:db/id 17592186125020 :question/id #uuid "4903eb08-1095-52c0-bd3a-a8d7c39455f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36918"} {:db/id 17592186125022 :question/id #uuid #uuid "e8d807a6-7896-5045-a14a-908b58831340" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes"}] :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)= (y-4)\ln (x-2),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\frac{y-4}{x-2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2} &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf  0$ at the point $(3,4).$"} {:db/id 17592186560256} {:db/id 17592186124944 :question/id #uuid "da858976-fa9b-559a-a71d-31223d9b1ce7" :question/math-academy-id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ find the points $(x,y),$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-1,0)$
- **II.** $(0,\frac{\pi}{2})$
- **III.** $(1,0)$
- **IV.** $(1,\frac{\pi}{2})$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{cases}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇f(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186385536 :question/id #uuid "191461eb-d37c-55af-a5cc-b1cdcbe5989a" :question/math-academy-id "q-71437" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124445 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e8d807a6-7896-5045-a14a-908b58831340" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f709b8d-e22d-555e-8f82-4b819b741a2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(0,0)" :db/id 17592186385538} {:answer/id #uuid "4f628e18-1e56-5031-998e-e94575d669fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-2,-1)" :db/id 17592186385539} {:answer/id #uuid "8a817cfe-6e50-5534-9c89-401a91beed6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(4,2)" :db/id 17592186385540} {:answer/id #uuid "6f89f99e-c222-5f75-b88f-1f3ed3be632f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(4,-2)" :db/id 17592186385541} {:answer/id #uuid "55d2d586-a13f-55b7-99b9-71d0fd4b3d5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(2,1)" :db/id 17592186385542}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2f709b8d-e22d-555e-8f82-4b819b741a2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(0,0)" :db/id 17592186385538} :answer-field/id #uuid "c5955cf1-cc26-55ec-8c2a-34ff0cdd5429" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186385537}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y+0-2x \\  & =2(2y-x) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x+2y-0 \\  & =2(2x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
2(2y-x)\,i+2(2x+y)\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y-x &=0 \\ 2x+y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y)+y & =0 \\ 5y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get $x=2\cdot 0=0.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point $(0,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186385543 :question/id #uuid "ceb4f40b-ddfe-5165-8e9a-092d10842d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-71475" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124445 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e8d807a6-7896-5045-a14a-908b58831340" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00852e0a-f6f6-5c5a-ac0e-5aab7917034a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(0,0,0)" :db/id 17592186385545} {:answer/id #uuid "0a138de7-1cdb-5fca-ab9b-192f03014909" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(e,e,e)" :db/id 17592186385546} {:answer/id #uuid "4db23065-4328-5f87-98fa-c2f53e71285d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{e},\frac{1}{e},\frac{1}{e})" :db/id 17592186385547} {:answer/id #uuid "c45fae02-a3c6-5e5b-83c3-515185ddf33b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-1,-1,-1)" :db/id 17592186385548} {:answer/id #uuid "965bb97e-ab1f-5bcd-b8b9-68650da44bfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(1,1,1)" :db/id 17592186385549}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "965bb97e-ab1f-5bcd-b8b9-68650da44bfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(1,1,1)" :db/id 17592186385549} :answer-field/id #uuid "12e34691-896f-5bb6-afac-57e259bb49f6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186385544}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇g(x,y,z)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0+0-1-0-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{1}{y}+0-0-1-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+0+\operatorname{ln}⁡z+z\cdot \frac{1}{z}-0-0-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=1.$  Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $∇g(x,y,z)=0$ at the point $(1,1,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186395845 :question/id #uuid "7795ea1b-86ec-5a3d-baba-dbdd67574697" :question/math-academy-id "q-36911"} {:db/id 17592186400373 :question/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇f(x,y,z)=0.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

- **I.** $(-1,-1,-1)$
- **II.** $(-1,-1,1)$
- **III.** $(-1,1,-1)$
- **IV.** $(-1,1,1)$
- **V.** $(1,-1,-1)$
- **VI.** $(1,1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}+0-\frac{1}{z{x}^{2}}-0 \\  & =-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}+0-0 \\  & =-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =0+0-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}x}-1 \\  & =-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}=0 \\ -\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}=0\end{cases}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=-1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x} & =0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}(-1)}{{z}^{2}(-1)} & =0 \\ 1-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{(-1)^{2}yz} & =0 \\ z+y & =0 \\ y & =-z\end{aligned}
$$

When $z=1,$ we have $y=-1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y=1.$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$"} {:db/id 17592186437020 :question/id #uuid "c3503a39-2405-5c8f-9ad7-2d39b5c187d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-128513"} {:db/id :knowledge-point/id #uuid "67cfec73-130c-5b68-a2e0-5f12837bfc81" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient"}] :question/problem "Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y) g(x,y)$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\sqrt{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f  + f \, \nabla\! g.
$$

Using the product rule shown above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186524196} {:db/id 17592186124954 :question/id #uuid "7958e50f-73b4-5252-b8f0-e891d3332089" :question/math-academy-id "q-36144"} {:db/id 17592186125073 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }i+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }i+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }j \\  & =\text{ }i+\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186383104 :question/id #uuid "fb82a957-3ae8-5e58-8924-0d152fcf4c22" :question/math-academy-id "q-128532"} {:db/id 17592186385550 :question/id #uuid made up of partial derivatives, we can expect it to have properties that are similar to partial derivatives.

Assume that $f$ and $g$ are functions whose first-order partial derivatives exist and are continuous on some open domain, and that $a,b,$ and $c$ are real constants. Then, the gradient has the following properties:

- Constant rule:  $\nabla c = \mathbf 0$

- Linearity: $\nabla (af + bg) = a \nabla\! f + b\nabla\! g$

- Product Rule: $\nabla(fg) = g \nabla\! f + f \nabla\! g$

- Quotient Rule: $\nabla \left( \dfrac{f}{g}\right) = \dfrac{ g \nabla\! f - f \nabla\! g}{g^2}$" :tutorial/id #uuid "52036b8f-4d6f-5609-bbcf-fc34a51d9b98" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2401 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Gradient"} :step/id #uuid "d4e8b345-fc40-5dfb-ab00-d4b25041d02c" :step/math-academy-id 10581 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125281}} {:db/id 17592186125281 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124447 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124251 :question/id #uuid "67e9bcb5-4bf2-56b8-8d82-95355841eaaa" :question/math-academy-id "e-3150"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "67cfec73-130c-5b68-a2e0-5f12837bfc81" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048813}] :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186524196} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124954} {:db/id 17592186125073} {:db/id 17592186262920} {:db/id 17592186262921} {:db/id 17592186335800} {:db/id 17592186338952} {:db/id 17592186383104} {:db/id 17592186385550} {:db/id 17592186437018} {:db/id 17592186524155} {:db/id 17592186524157} {:db/id 17592186524174} {:db/id 17592186524177} {:db/id 17592186524179} {:db/id 17592186524183} {:db/id 17592186524187} {:db/id 17592186524193}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient"} :step/id #uuid "acd8b544-63b3-5271-9729-c95afd0bee1d" :step/math-academy-id 10701 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125462}} {:db/id 17592186125462 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125806 :tutorial/content "For a multivariable function, the existence of the gradient implies continuity.

$Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables." :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-0\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,P=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186400902 :question/id #uuid "2172cdc2-fb35-5393-84ba-3c3dbc3c7926" :question/math-academy-id "q-140997"} {:db/id 17592186404766 :question/id #uuid $$

$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,D=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$" :question/worked-solution "Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-1)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186395003 :question/id #uuid "f3b5dfdd-d519-5388-b5ca-0b0271c9801c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95100" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162007 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.

17592186162854 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163229 :tutorial/content "Consider a quadratic form 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. As we know, any symmetric matrix can be orthogonally diagonalized as follows:

$$
D = P^T \! AP,
$$

where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix and $D$ is a diagonal matrix that contains eigenvalues of $A$ on the main diagonal. 

Now, substituting the change of variable $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}$ into our quadratic form, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}\,AP)y \\  & ={y}^{T}\,Dy,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives us a canonical form. 

As a result, using the orthogonal diagonalization of $A,$ we can find the canonical form of $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}.$

For example, let's find the canonical form of 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+4x_1x_2+x_2^2.
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/43/43e0dc28161c0564a75f6ea2dc7f0e09ad74dffae05b864e13c61330221f2983.svg)

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

![](images/c9/c93cabd6a18df429b5aad99815b23e337c17b88a1c271dd17344631dfc5f8ebb.svg)

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3y_1^2 - y_2^2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "26652f7d-7ad4-54a0-b4a6-5d9faafa8403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6a819afd-fa45-5c12-8319-bbdf2452f54b" :step/math-academy-id divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{ln⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}ln⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =ln⁡1-ln⁡8 \\  & =0-ln⁡8 \\  & =-ln⁡8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{ln⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{ln⁡8}+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186297341 :question/id #uuid "a909a720-f9c7-52e5-a8a4-abd3492e6b5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-31249"} {:db/id 17592186064177 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 312} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065407 :tutorial/content "Remember that the exponential function $e^x$ has the special property that the derivative of the exponential function is the exponential function itself. In other words, taking the derivative doesn't change anything, and we have

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm d x} \left(e^ x\right)  = e^ x.
$$

Since integration is the opposite of differentiation, and differentiating the exponential function leaves it unchanged, integrating the exponential function also leaves it unchanged. So, the integral of the exponential function is

Level Surface of a Function"}] :question/problem "Find the family of surfaces that describe the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y, z) = \ln(x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2).$" :question/worked-solution "The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{e}^{c}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$

"Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z) = \sin{xyz}$ that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the value of the function at $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
  f\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&= \sin \left(\pi\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = 1}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡xyz & =1 \\ xyz & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi k\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is any integer.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is the surface $xyz= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k,$ where $k$ is any integer."} {:db/id 17592186129604 $$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot e)-\sqrt{1\cdot 1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)-\sqrt{xy} & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz) & =\sqrt{xy} \\ xyz & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}} \\ z & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1978} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186130016 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130370 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following function: 

$$
w = f(x,y,z) =x^2 +y^2+z^2
$$

Sadly, it is impossible to plot this function because four spatial dimensions ($x,y,z,$ and $w$) are needed, and space as we know it is restricted to three dimensions. 

However, we can get an idea of how the function $f(x,y,z)$ behaves by plotting surfaces of the form

$$
\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3 \, : \,f(x,y,z)=c\right\},
$$

where $c$ is some value that is in the range of $f.$ These sets are called **level surfaces** because they can be visualized as surfaces in three-dimensional space, and are "level" in the sense that each surface corresponds to a constant value of $w.$

For this particular function, all level surfaces are spheres. For example, if we let $w = 4,$ we get

$$
x^2 +y^2+z^2 = 4,
$$

which is a sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](images/12/12de396a8460b929f656a44d701752e248180f926f22a5f5c3eeecf355e9f31a.png)

Functions with more than two input variables are sometimes called **hypersurfaces** because they can be thought of as surfaces that exist within a space whose dimension is greater than $3.$ For example, the function 

$$
w = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

can be thought of as a sphere in four-dimensional space, and is sometimes called a **hypersphere.**

Another way of thinking about the level surfaces of this function is that they correspond to the intersection of the hypersphere $w=x^2+y^2+z^2$ and the **hyperplane** $w=c.$" :tutorial/id #uuid Another way of thinking about the level surfaces of this function is that they correspond to the intersection of the hypersphere $w=x^2+y^2+z^2$ and the **hyperplane** $w=c.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0682086d-c964-557f-930b-8d2c1ebfd879" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3818 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5af3abd2-cf0a-5230-8fd4-5f285e096712" :step/math-academy-id 22162 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130019}} {:db/id 17592186130370 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following function: 

$$
w = f(x,y,z) =x^2 +y^2+z^2
$$

Sadly, it is impossible to plot this function because four spatial dimensions ($x,y,z,$ and $w$) are needed, and space as we know it is restricted to three dimensions. 

However, we can get an idea of how the function $f(x,y,z)$ behaves by plotting surfaces of the form

$$
\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3 \, : \,f(x,y,z)=c\right\},
$$

where $c$ is some value that is in the range of $f.$ These sets are called **level surfaces** because they can be visualized as surfaces in three-dimensional space, and are "level" in the sense that each surface corresponds to a constant value of $w.$

For this particular function, all level surfaces are spheres. For example, if we let $w = 4,$ we get

$$
x^2 +y^2+z^2 = 4,
$$

which is a sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](images/12/12de396a8460b929f656a44d701752e248180f926f22a5f5c3eeecf355e9f31a.png)

Functions with more than two input variables are sometimes called **hypersurfaces** because they can be thought of as surfaces that exist within a space whose dimension is greater than $3.$ For example, the function 

$$
w = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

can be thought of as a sphere in four-dimensional space, and is sometimes called a **hypersphere.**

Another way of thinking about the level surfaces of this function is that they correspond to the intersection of the hypersphere $w=x^2+y^2+z^2$ and the **hyperplane** $w=c.$" :tutorial/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ef96fb6f-8651-5bcd-8700-e66e3e1a4bf5" :question/math-academy-id "q-129189" :question/problem "Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-z$ that passes through the point $P(0,-2,4).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2,4) & ={2}^{2}-{0}^{2}-4 \\  & =4-0-4 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(0,-2,4)$ is the hyperbolic paraboloid $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "a94aecad-6d06-5584-9ae6-ff5e4c972c6e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409927}} {:db/id 17592186409924 :step/content {:db/id 17592186409920 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "90d9747b-5cb9-522d-836f-d3553c78f3a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of planes: $x+y-{z}^{2}-\sqrt{c}=0$" :db/id 17592186409906} {:answer/id #uuid "b986da89-36d0-55a1-8a48-c9bd757d18db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of spheres: ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}={c}^{2}$" :db/id 17592186409907} {:answer/id #uuid "c52cd181-65a2-5882-be1e-55e40ba886c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of hyperboloids of one sheet: ${c}^{2}{x}^{2}+{c}^{2}{y}^{2}-{c}^{2}{z}^{2}=1$" :db/id 17592186409909} {:answer/id #uuid "d11d59ab-ca32-5bdd-988e-9f236a634db6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of planes: $x+y+z\pm \sqrt{c}=0$" :db/id 17592186409910} {:answer/id #uuid "e4bedb04-7179-51c0-917b-125bf66e2a73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of surfaces given by $z=(x+y+c)^{2}$" :db/id 17592186409912}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409910} :answer-field/id #uuid "44405f81-ea2c-5ec0-9035-361601af3ea6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409917}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "00fd1a7d-44b2-529b-bcff-08a778520166" :question/math-academy-id "q-71586" :question/problem "Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=(x+y+z)^{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ (x+y+z)^{2} & =c \\ x+y+z & =\pm \sqrt{c} \\ x+y+z\pm \sqrt{c} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)$ can't be negative. Therefore, we get a family of planes:

$$
x+y+z\pm \sqrt{c}=0,\,c\in [0,\infty ).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bfbdcc24-f373-559b-9261-b97d80ffba78" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409925}} {:db/id 17592186409925 :step/content {:db/id 17592186409921 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7161819e-ecce-539e-a7d9-dd1392ee66bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=0" :db/id 17592186409905} {:answer/id #uuid "bf6e5c59-e63b-5d91-add0-3fc776b81f35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=0" :db/id 17592186409908} {:answer/id #uuid "f1e2ddba-6b1f-50a3-8f82-6a0e5406e403" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=0" :db/id 17592186409913} {:answer/id #uuid "f41b80f9-1883-5d0f-a39d-6bf74d468448" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z=0" :db/id 17592186409914} {:answer/id #uuid "fab3e1ad-3d44-56bd-8a1c-54fb07d88d5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=0" :db/id 17592186409916}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409905} :answer-field/id #uuid "e10467a3-d69e-5402-aad3-4b64333f090a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409919}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "595252cd-1afe-5f16-ae97-13c476966ff1" :question/math-academy-id "q-71594" :question/problem "Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}$ that passes through the point $P(2,\sqrt{5},3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,\sqrt{5},3) & =\frac{(2)^{2}}{2(2)^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}-(3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{4} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(2,\sqrt{5},3)$ is the surface ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=0.$"} :step/id #uuid "d981e48e-0b28-5d2c-b93e-70be17e1dbbd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409926}} {:db/id 17592186409926 :step/content {:db/id 17592186338966 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "341c06af-d1ba-5272-bb61-52ad376125d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}+2" :db/id 17592186336522} {:answer/id #uuid "5700ae9e-968d-5bb9-b16c-fb2495caa581" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-2" :db/id 17592186336830} {:answer/id #uuid "726140df-5488-5e91-b878-03e0a7dc18a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186337057} {:answer/id #uuid "caa01bba-d8dc-529e-84eb-7a172fdebb43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186337815} {:answer/id #uuid "f1709cb8-4e61-5ab7-a2f4-a614c896f494" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186338145}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337815} :answer-field/id #uuid "8165f0ea-43de-5434-a42c-9e10144a7415" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338506}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e38a7de1-ef3c-50e7-9539-8728abb34f00" :question/math-academy-id "q-71597" :question/problem "Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=z-4{x}^{2}-6{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point $P(2,1,22).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,22) & =22-4(2)^{2}-6(1)^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ z-4{x}^{2}-6{y}^{2} & =0 \\ z & =4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(2,1,22)$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z=4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "f363fade-7d87-58eb-bf21-09d29aa00dc3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409923}} {:db/id 17592186409927 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262977 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07f39980-6ad0-53d7-ad63-fbb34a382f5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of elliptic paraboloids: $z={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+C$" :db/id 17592186259949} {:answer/id #uuid "1456f86c-f369-5c8a-aa73-f917e987fcd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of elliptic cones: ${z}^{2}={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+C$" :db/id 17592186260057} {:answer/id #uuid "64d0fc97-78ec-5077-acfa-96dd790ebb7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of elliptic paraboloids: $z=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+C$" :db/id 17592186260745} {:answer/id #uuid "9b989c09-44c2-5eab-8bb7-5a6b7ceb875f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of planes: $z=x+3y+C$" :db/id 17592186261222} {:answer/id #uuid "a1c9051c-074f-5a24-a621-b2a3449ab493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A family of hyperbolic paraboloids: $z={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+C$" :db/id 17592186261283}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186259949} :answer-field/id #uuid "653d007f-928b-501b-88fc-8c02a0e38f08" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262296}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9849d588-2a95-5d11-993e-dd1a8d5d4837" :question/math-academy-id "q-129196" :question/problem "Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+z+3?$" :question/worked-solution "The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4,2,1) & ={4}^{2}+3(2-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}=18\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=18.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+3(y-1)^{2}-{z}^{2} & =18 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{18}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{6}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{18} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/99/99bb0ea67859fbd109442fcf698427ea43452087b4523b7202a760a2a8b27052.png)" :question/worked-solution "We can calculate the surface area of a sphere using the formula

$$
S = 4 \pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting

$$
S=50\pi \: \textrm{cm}^2
$$

into the formula, we can solve for $r$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= 4πr^{2} \\
50π &= 4πr^{2} \\
\frac{50π}{4π} &= r^{2} \\
r^{2} &= \frac{25}{2} \\
r &= \sqrt{\frac{25}{2}} \\
&= \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\
&= \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}cm
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048187} {:db/id 17592186049066} {:db/id 17592186120084 :question/id #uuid "07bfac0c-6848-5bbd-9ade-a9d61452156a" :question/math-academy-id "q-107389"} {:db/id 17592186120085 :question/id #uuid "56eea009-e0fb-5fb9-8191-486a4d7043ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-107392"} {:db/id 17592186119973 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119721 :question/id #uuid "acdb3e99-89dd-5463-871e-e4d5d370c827" :question/math-academy-id "e-9008"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5161a164-780d-5876-a8e2-458105dc8cab" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049059} {:db/id 17592186049953}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120083 :question/id #uuid "bdbc1ca6-1234-5709-a22d-e8172053f36d" :question/math-academy-id "q-107369"} {:db/id 17592186120160 :question/id #uuid "f5f6096a-9f0b-5a0b-9769-11bd82723ce9" :question/math-academy-id "q-19366"}] :knowledge-point/title "Relating the Surface Area and Volume of a Sphere"} {:db/id 17592186119721 :question/id #uuid "acdb3e99-89dd-5463-871e-e4d5d370c827" :question/math-academy-id "e-9008" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119973 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5161a164-780d-5876-a8e2-458105dc8cab" :knowledge-point/title "Relating the Surface Area and Volume of a Sphere"}] :question/problem "The volume of the sphere is $\dfrac{500}{3}\pi \: \textrm{in}^3$. Calculate the surface area of the sphere." :question/worked-solution "We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula

$$
V = \dfrac 4 3 \pi r^3
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting

$$
V=\dfrac{500}{3}\pi \: \textrm{in}^3
$$

into the formula, we can solve for $r$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= \frac{4}{3}πr^{3} \\
\frac{500}{3}π &= \frac{4}{3}πr^{3} \\
\frac{500π \cdot 3}{3 \cdot 4π} &= r^{3} \\
r^{3} &= 125 \\
r &= 5in
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the surface area of ​​the sphere is

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= 4πr^{2} \\
&= 4π(5)^{2} \\
&= 100πin^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049059} {:db/id 17592186049953} {:db/id 17592186120083 :question/id #uuid "bdbc1ca6-1234-5709-a22d-e8172053f36d" :question/math-academy-id "q-107369"} {:db/id 17592186120160 :question/id #uuid "f5f6096a-9f0b-5a0b-9769-11bd82723ce9" :question/math-academy-id "q-19366"} {:db/id 17592186049315} {:db/id 17592186049658} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186120962} :activity/id #uuid "796e396f-0c48-5eaf-a61f-e8b2d3339d65" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050966 :topic/id #uuid "76391ee0-ed5a-5ed3-8cef-c09827219e58" :topic/math-academy-id 1765} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120962 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121089 :tutorial/content "Given a sphere with radius

$$
r=4\:\textrm{cm}
$$

how do we calculate its surface area?

![](images/bd/bd7da8538c268a1dd9e17dc8f4185ba3db5847dca21d1eb408d0af2683ba64d4.png)

We can calculate the surface area $S$ of a sphere using the formula

$$
S = 4\pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting

$$
r=4\:\textrm{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
S = 4 \pi (4)^2 = 64\pi \:\textrm{cm}^2
$$

We often express the surface area of a sphere as a multiple of $\pi$. We can also get a numerical approximation using a calculator. In this case, we have

$$
S \approx 201.06 \:\textrm{cm}^2
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "1896920b-682d-58fe-874e-43fed82f00a0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5396 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186119990} {:db/id 17592186120962 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121089 :tutorial/content "Given a sphere with radius

$$
r=4\:\textrm{cm}
$$

how do we calculate its surface area?

![](images/bd/bd7da8538c268a1dd9e17dc8f4185ba3db5847dca21d1eb408d0af2683ba64d4.png)

We can calculate the surface area $S$ of a sphere using the formula

$$
S = 4\pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting

$$
r=4\:\textrm{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
S = 4 \pi (4)^2 = 64\pi \:\textrm{cm}^2
$$

We often express the surface area of a sphere as a multiple of $\pi$. We can also get a numerical approximation using a calculator. In this case, we have

$$
S \approx 201.06 \:\textrm{cm}^2
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "1896920b-682d-58fe-874e-43fed82f00a0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5396 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7fdd147a-47dd-5a6f-b15f-9c57770ebdeb" :step/math-academy-id 69030 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120963}} {:db/id 17592186121089 :tutorial/content "Given a sphere with radius

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3(-5) & =1 \\ -2{x}_{1} & =-14 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 3(7)+5(-5) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ which means

$$
7{a}_{1}-5{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=7+(-5)=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240991 :question/id #uuid "d5149dd7-ead1-5d7c-a754-e514e2e6e606" :question/math-academy-id "q-105167"} {:db/id 17592186317259 :question/id #uuid "8179ffc2-2381-5ec9-a386-111d6e4cae85" :question/math-academy-id "q-34242"} {:db/id 17592186342116 :question/id #uuid "0008ebd1-cf28-5d38-a9cd-5c6dde0f95a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-73951"} {:db/id 17592186342117 :question/id #uuid "eec4fe83-c254-5d51-9484-b88391578898" :question/math-academy-id "q-73952"} {:db/id 17592186342118 :question/id #uuid "abf235b3-2d59-5bfb-aea0-aa237461f6b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-73954"} {:db/id 17592186342123 :question/id #uuid "3c67076c-502b-504a-869c-d6e3549e0a05" :question/math-academy-id "q-73981"} {:db/id 17592186435825 :question/id #uuid "e9e20ff9-23b3-5457-a430-304f98c0d839" :question/math-academy-id "q-73950" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fdd8247-3e99-5680-9837-f81ce2e4daa8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186435812} {:answer/id #uuid "6588aecf-5be8-5075-92ab-05e2c0bd205f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186435816} {:answer/id #uuid "877b327c-7099-5b51-a1a0-e54f12c801d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186435818} {:answer/id #uuid "9a314fbe-bce0-5c72-becd-d86fdd89cb4c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186435819} {:answer/id #uuid "b6573507-37c6-5328-ab6e-7644606e55a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186435821}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435819} :answer-field/id #uuid "50ab6af3-7838-5baf-b926-7d20ec2e1151" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435822}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-2 \\ -{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=5 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -5 \\ 0 & -3 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-2 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-5 \\ 0 &=-12.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

However, the final equation $0=-12$  gives a false statement. So the system has no solution."} {:db/id 17592186342132 :question/id #uuid "6ca28715-77ca-55f5-9aad-4851b6f70f79" :question/math-academy-id "q-74028"} {:db/id 17592186342133 :question/id #uuid "237520c7-3369-5c34-87a7-ba4be3c9b705" :question/math-academy-id "q-74032" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0dd1e2d3-3d25-597c-a847-faa140432c9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186339255} {:answer/id #uuid "28a2b981-6db8-5f16-b21b-6ae088a23e3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186339484} {:answer/id #uuid "309c51a6-6646-55e5-a9ef-db0cd36bd5b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186339553} {:answer/id #uuid "732f8930-5de1-53c0-8f9f-0564fc2ea176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186340149} {:answer/id #uuid "d7a94670-179b-5241-8088-b40d00d22100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186341041}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339553} :answer-field/id #uuid "95f0dc3f-6280-5dbc-ad92-0375cafd9b79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$

$$
{a}_{1}-2{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=b.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3(-5) & =1 \\ -2{x}_{1} & =-14 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 3(7)+5(-5) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ which means

$$
7{a}_{1}-5{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=7+(-5)=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "130d098a-c26b-57ed-9a17-40b7cc7b707e"} {:db/id 17592186435827 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435824 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b3b3e4e-ca03-5bf0-b918-e879378cf4f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186435813} {:answer/id #uuid "3e56b548-f823-5efc-89ba-5bfa7fe486df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186435814} {:answer/id #uuid "62cff3cd-01fc-5c8d-bb73-00c6490598f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-11" :db/id 17592186435815} {:answer/id #uuid "7f4f8e1e-a357-552c-aea0-48de6f4f316a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186435817} {:answer/id #uuid "a0c118c7-81b9-5bfc-90ce-dd9634f5f92e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186435820}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435814} :answer-field/id #uuid "a66e7a5d-9617-5080-a5e0-b50e86007465" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435823}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e8bdc664-5423-57fc-a753-871b318d24e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-34598" :question/problem "Find the value of ${x}_{1}-{x}_{2}$ given that  $4a+3x=b$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -11 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -18 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{3} \\ -11{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -18 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{2}-11{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -18 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ -2{x}_{2}-11{x}_{3} &=-18 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -15 & -30\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{15}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=-6 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this value into  the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}-2(2)=-6\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-2.
$$

 

Finally, by substituting ${x}_{2}=-2$ and ${x}_{3}=2$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} & =5 \\ {x}_{1}+(-2)+3(2) & =5 \\ {x}_{1}+4 & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=1$, ${x}_{2}=-2$, and ${x}_{3}=2,$ which means 

$$
{a}_{1}-2{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1+(-2)+2=1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35ab3d0c-3feb-5eb0-8af0-2d726c5cb861" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435826}} {:db/id 17592186435829 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342130 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ca1e367-7e59-5b69-861b-8c5df685d98a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186339240} {:answer/id #uuid "70e98200-2ef8-5fee-9135-1a64cdf08565" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186340130} {:answer/id #uuid "a0f91210-c308-5ac5-8b5f-ecea8232309c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186340589} {:answer/id #uuid "cd78319b-964c-5a76-83e0-5cc4ba5b698b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186340951} {:answer/id #uuid "d5c0ee9d-d678-5d90-ac70-ae36c44cd666" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186341020}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340951} :answer-field/id #uuid "d6466acd-a8cc-51d2-bb7d-d48bfacf96c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341757}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ff5142a4-ab7b-5300-baa5-14f6253ed7fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-74006" :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{64}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{8}^{2}}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {8}^{-2}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {8}^{n-3}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2\,000\,000.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {8}^{n-3} & >2\,000\,000 \\ {8}^{n-3} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({8}^{n-3}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ (n-3)\operatorname{log}⁡(8) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ n-3 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(8)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(8)}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (1\,000\, 000)} {\log (8)} + 3 \approx 9.643.
$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "The first term of the sequence is $a_1=16,$ and the common ratio is

$$
